executive_summary: The dollar enters October at its strongest level in a year. EUR/USD closed at 1.1243 on 2026-10-01, the lowest close of the past 52 weeks (0th percentile of the range), and the DXY computed from the gated price store on the ICE formula stood at 102.04, the highest close of the past year and 2.48% above its level of 2026-09-02; over three months the DXY is up 1.15%, over six months 3.03% and over one year 3.02%, while the Fed's broad trade-weighted index was 120.33 on 2026-09-25. The dominant narrative is a hawkish Fed meeting an energy shock: the FOMC hiked 25bp to 3.75-4.00% on 2026-09-16 by 12-0 under Chair Warsh, the median dot puts the funds rate at 4.1% at end-2026 and end-2027, the 2-year Treasury yields 4.78% and the 10-year 5.24% (99th percentile of its one-year range), Q2 GDP was revised up to 2.2% annualised and August payrolls rose 162,000, while the seven-month US-Israeli war on Iran holds Brent near $103 and headline PCE at 3.4%. Valuation is modestly expensive: the BIS real effective dollar of 106.70 (August 2026) sits 6.7% above its 2020 base, yet at the 9th percentile of its January-2024-onward range, so the rally is a rate repricing from a cheapened starting point rather than an overshoot. The key tension is that every peer central bank is tightening too - the ECB, BoJ, RBA, RBNZ and Norges Bank all hiked between 2 and 29 September - so the dollar's rate advantage is near its peak while the twin deficits (current account -3.0% of GDP, federal deficit about 6% of GDP) and a falling reserve share (56.70%) keep the structural flow negative. We are Bullish tactically (conviction 3, net score +0.3782, rank 1 of 11) because rates, data momentum and a fresh $12.5bn speculative build dominate the next four weeks into the 2026-10-28 FOMC, and Bearish strategically (conviction 2, net score -0.1822, rank 8 of 11) because the Fed's dots are flat through 2027 while peers keep hiking, and the external and fiscal factors carry the higher strategic weights. Our six-month EUR/USD target is 1.1550 (DXY about 99.5), below the 1.18-1.20 bank consensus for end-2026; the caveat is that an escalation in the Gulf or a funding squeeze would push the dollar to the left side of the smile and invalidate the strategic call.

Volatility stayed low - EUR/USD realised vol of 4.08% - so the move was a grind rather than a spike, with high-yield spreads widening 59bp to 324bp as the only sign of stress. The regime is now testing whether the Fed's 'no urgency' message from Williams on 2026-09-29 caps the move.

tactical.analysis: The Fed's target range of 3.75-4.00% (effective 3.88%, SOFR 3.87% on 2026-10-01) ranks third in G10+SGD behind the RBA at 4.60% and Norges Bank at 4.50%, and on the 3.875% midpoint the dollar out-yields seven of ten peers: +387.5bp over CHF, +262.5bp over JPY, +212.5bp over SEK, +162.5bp over CAD, +137.5bp over the ECB deposit rate, +112.5bp over NZD and +12.5bp over GBP, while paying 72.5bp to AUD and 62.5bp to NOK [1][36][37][38]. The 2-year Treasury at 4.78% sits 90.5bp above the effective funds rate and 158bp above the 3.20% German 2-year, so the front end already discounts at least one more 25bp hike. The 10-year rose 45bp in September to 5.24%, its 99th percentile of the past year and near its highest since 2007, which is 172bp above Bunds, about 214bp above JGBs and 18bp below gilts [15][17][18][19]. The curve bear-steepened: 2s10s widened from +40bp to +46bp and 3m10s reached +107bp, the top of its one-year range, driven by real yields (10-year TIPS 2.88%, +44bp in a month) rather than breakevens (2.36%, flat). For the next meeting on 2026-10-28, October hike odds were about 66% on 2026-09-25 and fell below 50% on CME FedWatch after NY Fed President Williams said on 2026-09-29 that 'there is no need for urgency' while a further increase 'may be appropriate late this year' [7][8]. Our probabilities are 35% hike / 65% hold for October and 70% for a cumulative 25bp by the 2026-12-09 SEP meeting, which matches the 12 of 18 participants whose dots show a 4.125% midpoint at year-end [6][2]; on our path the 3-month expected midpoint is about 4.00% and the 6-month about 4.10%, within 5bp of the market's path, so the level is fairly priced. Every peer except the SNB and BoC is tightening - the ECB, BoJ, RBA, RBNZ and Norges Bank all hiked between 2 and 29 September and the BoE is about 80% priced for 2026-11-05 - so over four weeks the forward differential is stable rather than widening. The tactical case therefore rests on the real-yield channel: each 10bp rise in the 10-year has been worth 0.21% on the DXY over the past 60 sessions (correlation +0.32), and the October data calendar (CPI on 2026-10-14) is more likely to add to than subtract from front-end yields. Carry adds little at this horizon: the 137.5bp EUR/USD differential is worth about 13 pips a month against a 58-pip daily ATR, so this is a rates-momentum signal, not a carry trade.

We expect a hold in October and a December hike, so the level is fairly priced and the tactical edge is directional: the October CPI and retail-sales prints are more likely to lift front-end and real yields than to lower them.

strategic.analysis: Over one to six months the question is the direction of the differential, not its level, and the direction turns against the dollar. The September SEP puts the median funds rate at 4.1% at end-2026, 4.1% at end-2027, 3.9% at end-2028 and 3.2% in the longer run, so the Fed sees itself within 25bp of its peak and then flat for a year [2]. Peers are earlier in their cycles: the ECB raised its deposit rate to 2.50% on 2026-09-10 and is 'not pre-committing' with inflation 'well above target for an extended period', the BoJ hiked to 1.25% by 7-2 with the JGB 10-year at a 30-year high near 3.1%, the BoE held 6-3 with three votes to hike, and the RBA reached 4.60% on 2026-09-29 [36][37][38][18]. If the ECB and BoJ each add 25bp by March 2027 and the Fed adds one, the dollar's differential against EUR stays at 137.5bp and against JPY at 262.5bp, but if the Fed stops at 4.00% the gaps narrow to 112.5bp and 237.5bp, and against GBP the dollar would move from +12.5bp to -12.5bp. The carry level still favours the dollar against seven of ten peers, with the best carry-to-vol against SGD (0.62 on the T-bill proxy), CHF (0.54) and CAD (0.38), and carry worked in September: USD/CHF rose 2.23% and USD/CAD 2.73% while the high-yielders AUD and NOK both lost to the dollar. Term structure argues the other way: a 10-year at 5.24% against a longer-run dot of 3.2% implies a term premium of roughly 100bp or more, the market charging for supply rather than for higher policy rates. The 6-month OIS-equivalent path we estimate at a 4.10% midpoint, versus our own 4.05%, a 5bp gap that is too small to trade. We hold Neutral at 55 because the dollar's carry cushion (third-highest policy rate, positive carry-to-vol against seven peers) offsets a forward differential that is more likely to narrow than widen; a December hike with a higher 2027 dot would break the stalemate in the dollar's favour, an ECB or BoJ hike without a Fed follow-through against it.

tactical.analysis: US data are strong on activity and mixed on inflation, which is the combination that keeps the Fed hawkish without forcing it to accelerate. Q2 GDP was revised up 0.7pp to 2.2% annualised in the third estimate on 2026-09-30, after 2.5% in Q1, with real consumer spending up 0.6% in August alone and nominal spending up 0.9% [11][10]. Payrolls rose 162,000 in August against a 55,000 consensus with 55,000 of upward revisions, unemployment held at 4.1% as the labour force grew 683,000, and average hourly earnings rose 3.1% y/y [14]. Leading indicators are expansionary: ISM manufacturing 54.5 in September with new orders 55.3, the S&P Global flash composite 58.4 and services 58.7, the Chicago PMI 58.8 and the Atlanta Fed GDPNow 3.7% for Q3, down from 5.1% in mid-September but still well above trend. Headline inflation is energy-driven: CPI 3.4% y/y with gasoline +3.9% in August accounting for over a third of the monthly rise, against core CPI of 2.4% [13]; the Fed's preferred core PCE was 3.0% y/y in August (0.2% m/m) and headline PCE 3.4%, both below the 3.3% and 3.7% consensus [10]. Cost-push is visible upstream - ISM prices paid 77.9, PPI 5.4% y/y, Michigan 1-year expectations 4.6% and 5-year 3.4% - so the risk is expectations-driven persistence rather than demand-pull. The soft spots are sentiment and housing: Conference Board confidence fell to 81.9 against an 89.2 forecast, Michigan sentiment is 48.1, JOLTS openings dropped to 7.079m and housing starts to 1.275m. Against the peers the growth gap is the dollar's best argument: US GDP of 2.1% y/y compares with 1.2% in the euro area, 1.4% in the UK and 0.7% in Japan, and US unemployment of 4.1% with 6.4% in the euro area and Canada. Surprises are balanced rather than one-sided: of 141 US releases with a forecast in September, 60 beat and 65 missed in economic terms, so the edge comes from levels, not from a surprise trend. For the 2026-10-14 September CPI we expect headline at 3.3-3.5% and core at 2.4-2.5%, broadly in line, so the tactical risk is a hawkish core surprise rather than a dovish one.

tactical.what_is_priced: Markets price the US expansion as durable - the 2-year at 4.78% and one more hike - and treat the inflation overshoot as energy. We expect the October data to confirm 2%-plus growth and core inflation at or above 3% on the PCE measure, which keeps the December hike priced and supports the dollar into the 2026-10-28 meeting.

strategic.analysis: Over six months the growth advantage persists but the inflation impulse that justified the hike fades, which leaves the factor balanced. The Fed's own projections have headline PCE falling from 3.7% in 2026 to 2.3% in 2027 and core PCE from 3.4% to 2.5%, with unemployment flat at 4.1% and GDP 2.3-2.4% [2]; that is a soft landing at full employment, not an overheating economy that needs further tightening. Core CPI at 2.4% and core PCE at 3.0% are already below the SEP's 3.4% core PCE year-end projection, so the projection would have to be revised down unless the energy shock leaks into services [13][10]. The household side is under strain: the saving rate is 4.1%, real income growth is negative on a 3.4% headline deflator, confidence is at 81.9 and Michigan sentiment at 48.1, and GDPNow has fallen from 5.1% to 3.7% in two weeks. Housing is the weakest sector with the NAHB index at 32 and starts at 1.275m, as 30-year mortgage rates near 7% bite. On the other side, Q2 profits rose $384.0bn, capital spending is robust and the labour force grew 683,000 in August, so supply-side growth can sustain 2%-plus GDP without a wage spiral (earnings 3.1%) [11][14]. Relative growth still favours the US by about 0.9pp over the euro area and 1.4pp over Japan, which is the US-exceptionalism channel the currency brief identifies. We hold Neutral at 55: the growth gap supports the dollar, but disinflation in core measures and a softer consumer reduce the Fed's need to deliver more than the one hike already priced.

tactical.analysis: Risk appetite is split between resilient equities and deteriorating credit, and both halves currently help the dollar. The VIX closed at 16.39 on 2026-10-01, at the 34th percentile of its one-year range and unchanged on the month, while the S&P 500 at 7,666 is up 12.0% year to date and at the 88th percentile of its one-year range, and the Nasdaq 100 at 30,502 is up 20.8% year to date. Credit is the stress signal: the ICE BofA high-yield spread widened 59bp in a month to 324bp, the 98th percentile of its one-year range, and the investment-grade spread is 86bp, the 94th percentile [20]. On the dollar smile the US sits on the right-hand side - US exceptionalism with real yields at 2.88% - and the war with Iran, now seven months old with Brent near $103 and Hormuz crude flows about 80% of pre-war levels, supplies left-side optionality if credit stress becomes a funding event [16][15]. The dollar's measured beta to risk is mildly counter-cyclical: over the past 60 sessions the DXY's correlation with the S&P 500 was -0.31 (beta -0.14), with the 10-year yield +0.32 and with gold -0.53. That structure is intact: the dollar rose as yields rose and as gold fell 4.79% in a month, so the standard correlation regime has not broken down. The regime is transitioning from goldilocks to late-cycle: equities are pricing AI-led earnings while credit is pricing supply and energy costs, and the dollar wins in that divergence because it benefits from the rate side without needing a risk-off shock. Tail risks that would shift the regime are an escalation that closes Hormuz again (dollar-positive via the left side), a peace deal that drops Brent below $85 (dollar-negative via the bottom of the smile) and a Treasury auction failure that turns the bond sell-off into a US-specific risk premium (dollar-negative).

tactical.what_is_priced: Equity volatility is priced for calm (VIX at the 34th percentile) while credit has already repriced for stress (HY at the 98th percentile). We expect the credit message to dominate if the October data keep yields rising, which favours the dollar; the market has not priced a funding dimension to the credit widening.

strategic.analysis: Over one to six months the risk factor is a two-sided bet on the Gulf and on credit, and the dollar's exposure to the two tails is symmetrical. A negotiated reopening of Hormuz - the US and Iran held 'very productive' indirect talks at the UN General Assembly, though Trump rejected Iran's seven-day roadmap - would cut the energy premium, pull headline inflation down and move the dollar toward the bottom of the smile, where carry flows leave the dollar for higher-beta currencies [16]. A renewed closure would do the opposite through haven demand, as the closure at the war's peak, when tanker traffic fell to two a day, showed [16]. Credit is the second axis: high-yield spreads at 324bp have widened by 59bp in a month but remain only at the 72nd percentile of the past five years, so the widening is a repricing rather than a crisis. Equity leadership is narrow and US-centric - the Nasdaq 100 is up 20.8% year to date against 12.0% for the S&P 500 - which supports inflows into US assets while it lasts but creates a concentrated reversal risk. The VIX at 16.39 is at the 37th percentile of five years, so complacency, not fear, is the starting point. Taken together the probabilities balance: we put a 25% chance on a Gulf settlement within six months and a 20% chance on a renewed escalation, with the remainder a grinding stalemate in which risk sentiment is a background factor for the dollar. Neutral at 50 reflects that the six-month risk distribution has fat tails on both sides of the dollar smile.

tactical.analysis: Positioning is fresh and mid-range, which removes it as a contrarian signal in either direction. On the IMM speculative measure, speculators' aggregate dollar long against G10 currencies rose by $12.5bn to $18.4bn in the week to 2026-09-22, the first increase after seven weeks of reduction, with JPY sold by 48k contracts (-$3.9bn), EUR by 25.3k (-$3.6bn), GBP by 23.9k (-$2.0bn) and NZD by 21.9k (-$1.3bn), the largest NZD sale since 2018 [22]. StoneX measures the DXY-equivalent net long at $17.3bn and calls the $12.5bn build the fastest weekly increase in seven years [23]. In the disaggregated data cached for six contracts, leveraged funds flipped from 21,041 contracts net short the dollar on 2026-09-15 to 10,624 net long on 2026-09-22 (about $3.8bn), while asset managers cut their net dollar short from 124,429 to 27,310 contracts (about -$13.3bn), driven by a 35,215-contract cut in euro longs to 216,483. Combined, the two groups are about $9.5bn short the dollar, at the 44th percentile of the 25 cached weeks, against a range of -$31.5bn in May to +$24.7bn in late July. Open interest across the six contracts fell from 2.80m to 2.20m contracts on the September roll, so engagement is lower after the IMM date, not higher. Real-money flows are mixed: July TIC data show $83.7bn of total net inflows and $44.4bn of official long-term purchases, but private foreigners sold $3.7bn of long-term securities and the adjusted long-term total was -$27.9bn [25]. Options show dollar calls bid against the euro (1-month risk reversal -0.84 vol) and dollar puts bid against the yen (-2.43 vol), so hedgers expect the dollar to diverge by counterpart rather than move as a bloc. Neutral at 55: momentum in flows is dollar-positive, but at mid-range there is neither a squeeze to fuel nor a crowded long to unwind.

tactical.what_is_priced: The market has just started to rebuild dollar longs, so positioning prices the Fed hike but not a further leg of dollar strength. We expect the build to continue moderately into the 2026-10-28 FOMC, but the starting point is too neutral for positioning to add conviction either way.

strategic.analysis: Structural flows lean against the dollar over six months even though speculative positioning is neutral. The IMF's COFER data released on 2026-09-30 show the dollar's share of allocated reserves falling to 56.70% in 2026-Q2 from 57.18% in Q1, while the euro's rose to 20.60% from 20.04%; dollar claims were largely unchanged while euro holdings rose by about $100bn, so reserve managers added to the euro rather than selling dollars [24]. The asset-manager community remains structurally short the dollar through 216,483 contracts of euro longs, a position built as a hedge against US policy risk that has survived a 2.98% fall in EUR/USD in September. Private foreign investors were net sellers of US long-term securities in July (-$3.7bn) and the adjusted long-term total was -$27.9bn, with official buyers ($44.4bn) and Treasury bills ($38.8bn) carrying the inflow [25]. That composition - short-dated and official rather than long-dated and private - is the funding profile of a currency whose holders are shortening duration, not adding exposure. Hedge ratios are the swing factor: foreign holders of US assets who raise hedge ratios sell dollars forward, and a 5.24% 10-year with a falling dollar reserve share is the setting in which they do so. Against that, the speculative long of $18.4bn is below the late-July peak of the combined cached measure (+$24.7bn on 2026-07-28), so there is room for momentum money to add if the Fed hikes in December before positioning reaches the late-July extreme. Bearish at 50 reflects a slow structural drain rather than a positioning extreme.

factors.contrarian_analysis_tactical: Positioning is not stretched: the combined leveraged-plus-asset-manager dollar position is at the 44th percentile of its 25-week range and the IMM aggregate long of $18.4bn is well below the levels that marked past dollar tops; for the dollar, 'stretched' begins near the 85th-90th percentile because open interest is so large. The unwind trigger would be a soft US data print - payrolls below 50,000 or core CPI at or below 0.1% m/m - or Fed speakers pushing back on a December hike, which would reverse the $12.5bn weekly build as fast as it came in. A squeeze would be moderate but fast: the nearest analogue is the $29.4bn swing in the combined position from +$24.7bn on 2026-07-28 to -$4.7bn on 2026-08-25, which took EUR/USD up 2.5% from 1.1387 to 1.1675 in four weeks. The other side of the trade - asset managers long 216,483 euro contracts - is betting on ECB hikes and US fiscal risk; they are the natural sellers of euros if EUR/USD breaks 1.1170. Signal: neutral, with momentum favouring further dollar buying.
factors.contrarian_analysis_strategic: Over six months the contrarian case runs against the dollar only if speculators chase the move: a rebuild above $30bn, while reserve managers keep diversifying and asset managers keep their euro hedge, would leave the dollar long crowded into the December FOMC. The unwind triggers would be a Gulf settlement that removes the energy shock or a Fed that does not hike in December. The nearest analogue is this summer: the combined cached position peaked at +$24.7bn on 2026-07-28 with the DXY at 101.42, and the DXY fell 2.5% to 98.91 by 2026-08-25 as that long was cut to -$4.7bn. The other side - structural euro and yen longs - is backed by peers' hiking cycles and by the IMF's evidence of reserve managers adding euros. Signal: mildly bearish for the dollar at six months, conditional on positioning becoming crowded first.

tactical.analysis: The external balance is a structural negative that rarely matters over four weeks, and the energy shock gives the dollar a mild offset. The current-account deficit widened to $246.0bn in 2026-Q2, 3.0% of GDP, from $212.6bn (2.7%) in Q1, on a wider goods deficit partly offset by smaller primary and secondary income deficits [12]. The August goods trade deficit was $132.6bn against a $116.3bn forecast, so the Q3 current account is also likely to widen. The net international investment position is -$22.42tn (liabilities $69.39tn against assets $46.97tn), deeper than the currency brief's -$20tn benchmark [12]. Terms of trade are the offset: the US is a net energy exporter, WTI at $96.16 on 2026-09-29 is up 49.6% on the year, Henry Hub gas is $3.18 and Brent $102.59-103.16 (2026-09-29/30), so an oil shock is a mild dollar positive, unlike for EUR, JPY and GBP [15][16]. Trade policy has turned less restrictive for imports: the Supreme Court struck down the IEEPA tariffs on 2026-02-20, the 10% Section 122 replacement expired on 2026-07-24, and the effective tariff rate is about 7.2% with Section 232/301/338 tariffs covering 54% of imports, including 50% on Canada under Section 338 [30]. The trade-weighted mix shows the effect: the dollar is at a one-year high against the euro but USD/NOK is down 5.14% and AUD/USD up 6.86% on the year, the energy and metals exporters outperforming. Neutral at 55 because a wider deficit and an energy terms-of-trade gain roughly offset over a four-week horizon.

strategic.analysis: Over one to six months the external factor carries its full 0.16 weight and leans against the dollar. The current-account deficit has widened for two quarters to 3.0% of GDP while the federal deficit runs near 6% of GDP, the twin-deficit configuration the currency brief identifies as the setting in which the dollar's financing need becomes visible [12][26]. Financing has shifted toward short-dated and official money: July TIC data show official long-term purchases of $44.4bn and T-bill purchases of $38.8bn but private long-term sales of $3.7bn [25]. The reserve-currency cushion is still large - a 56.70% COFER share and the dollar's role in trade invoicing - but the share fell 0.48pp in one quarter and the euro gained 0.56pp [24]. The energy terms-of-trade gain is real but fragile: it depends on a war premium that a Hormuz settlement would remove, and on WTI staying near $90-100 rather than reverting to the $57-64 range of late 2025. Tariff revenue is falling after the IEEPA ruling and the expiry of Section 122, which reduces a source of fiscal income and removes the import-compression effect that narrowed the goods deficit in 2025 [30]. The NIIP at -$22.42tn means net income payments rise with every increase in US yields, eroding the 'dark matter' return advantage. Bearish at 55: a widening deficit financed increasingly by short-dated official flows, with a falling reserve share, is a slow structural drag that dominates the strategic horizon.

tactical.analysis: The Fed's communication has turned decisively hawkish and, more importantly for the dollar, credibly independent. The 2026-09-16 statement replaced conditional language with a commitment - 'The Committee will deliver price stability' - and described inflation as 'elevated', with the hike approved 12-0 [1][6]. Chair Warsh set this up at Jackson Hole, saying he 'would be hard pressed to describe broad financial conditions as restrictive', and delivered the first hike since July 2023 although President Trump demanded rates 'of 1%, or less' [6]. The Supreme Court's 2026-06-29 ruling in Trump v. Cook, which bars removal of a governor without notice, a response and a reviewable factual basis, has reduced the institutional-independence risk that weighed on the dollar earlier in the year [9]. The forward guidance is explicit through the dots: 12 of 18 participants see one more 25bp hike by December and four see two, and the median is 4.1% for both 2026 and 2027 [2][6]. Market pricing broadly accepts that guidance: October hike odds of about 66% on 2026-09-25 fell below 50% only after Williams, a permanent voter, said on 2026-09-29 that 'there is no need for urgency' and that one more increase 'may be appropriate late this year' [7][8]. On our estimate the gap between the market-implied and the median-dot path is within 5bp at end-2026, so markets are buying what the Fed is selling. The next communication events are the minutes of the September meeting on 2026-10-07, which will reveal how many participants argued for a faster pace, and the 2026-10-28 decision without projections. Bullish at 58: a central bank that hikes unanimously against political pressure supports the dollar's real-yield premium, and the minutes are more likely to sound hawkish than dovish given the 12-of-18 dot distribution.

strategic.analysis: Over six months credibility is the dollar's anchor against its fiscal and external weaknesses, but the guidance itself is not dollar-positive in direction. The SEP's 4.1% median for end-2027 and 3.9% for end-2028 tells the market the Fed expects to hold, not to lead, while the ECB says it is 'not pre-committing' and the BoJ and BoE are still tightening [2][36][37]. Credibility is what keeps that plateau from becoming a dollar-negative pivot narrative: breakevens are anchored at 2.36% (10-year) and 2.36% (5-year) despite headline PCE at 3.4%, and the 10-year TIPS yield of 2.88%, at the 99th percentile of its one-year range, is a real-rate premium the market only pays to a central bank it trusts to defend the target. Communication style under Warsh is less forward-guiding than under his predecessors - he declined to submit his own projection in June, consistent with his 'long-held views on the SEP' - which raises event volatility around each meeting but has not reduced trust. Political risk persists: Trump's public demand for 1% rates and the possibility of renewed attempts to remove governors through the procedure the Supreme Court set out are tail risks to independence [6][9]. Voting is cohesive - 12-0 in September - and the dissent risk is on the hawkish side, with four participants already projecting 4.375%. The key upcoming communications are the 2026-12-09 SEP, where a higher 2027 dot would extend the dollar's support, and the annual rotation of regional voters in January 2027. Bullish at 52: a credible Fed limits the term-premium and debasement narratives that would otherwise dominate the strategic dollar case.

tactical.analysis: Event risk over four weeks is dense but two-sided. The three dated events with the largest dollar impact are the 2026-10-14 CPI, the 2026-10-28 FOMC and the 2026-11-03 midterm elections, the last just outside the four-week window but inside the option tenor. The Gulf is the main geopolitical driver: the war with Iran began on 2026-02-28, Hormuz crude flows recovered to 9.719 mb/d in September, about 80% of pre-war exports, the US maintains a naval blockade, and Trump rejected Iran's seven-day reopening roadmap while describing the indirect talks as 'very productive' [16]. Balance-sheet runoff ended long ago: the FOMC decided on 2025-10-29 to conclude the reduction of its securities holdings on 2025-12-01, and since then reserve management purchases have added Treasury bills at $10bn a month, with all Treasury principal rolled over and agency principal reinvested in bills [4][32][3]. The H.4.1 for 2026-10-01 shows total assets of $6.743tn and reserve balances of $2.948tn on the 2026-09-30 Wednesday, up $17.9bn on the week and only $18bn lower than a year earlier; the weekly average was $2.881tn [5]. Money markets passed quarter-end without stress: SOFR printed 3.87% on 2026-10-01, 3bp below IORB at 3.90% and 13bp below the 4.00% standing repo rate, so there is no sign of reserve scarcity [3][21]. Bill supply is heavy - 3-month bills auctioned at 4.11% and 6-month at 4.285% on 2026-09-28, 24bp and 41bp above SOFR - which drains money-fund cash but also prices the December hike. That is a modest dollar funding premium concentrated in Japan, consistent with Japanese investors paying up to hedge dollar assets rather than with global dollar scarcity. On the dollar smile, funding is not pushing the dollar to the left side; the rally is a right-side rates story. Neutral at 55: liquidity is neither a tailwind nor a headwind for the dollar over four weeks.

Reserve management purchases at $10bn a month and the rollover of all Treasury principal grow the balance sheet slowly - total assets are $155.9bn higher than a year ago - and the implementation note instructs the Desk to buy bills 'as needed' to keep reserves ample [3][5][32]. Peer hikes compress the rate component of the basis: as the ECB, BoJ and BoE raise rates, the cost of hedging dollar assets falls for euro and yen investors, which encourages higher hedge ratios and dollar selling forward. The counter-argument is the year-end turn: the December funding date and a possible shutdown on 2026-12-11 that would distort the Treasury General Account could push the JPY basis below -50bp and briefly move the dollar toward the left side of the smile. Reserves at $2.948tn are close to the roughly $3tn level the currency brief cites as the minimum comfortable range, so a TGA rebuild could tighten conditions quickly. No swap-line usage or Senior Loan Officer Survey data were retrieved this cycle (documented gaps). Bearish at 50 because the Fed's operating framework is designed to prevent the kind of dollar shortage that would support the currency, while peers' hikes reduce the hedging cost that has kept foreign investors unhedged.

The key dates are the 2026-11-03 midterms, the 2026-11-05 BoE MPR, the 2026-12-09 FOMC SEP, the 2026-12-11 funding deadline, the 2026-12-17 ECB projections and the 2026-12-18 BoJ meeting. Conviction is limited to 2 because no strategic factor exceeds 58% confidence, the largest contributor (External Balance) moves slowly, and the Gulf can push the dollar to either side of the smile. The view differs from consensus in timing rather than direction: banks such as MUFG (EUR/USD 1.18 by Q4 2026, DXY 98.07) and Scotiabank (1.20) are bearish the dollar now, while we see a tactical rally first and a smaller decline later. Actionability is moderate: the cleanest expression is long JPY against the dollar, where the REER-relative valuation gap is largest (the dollar about 62% rich), the BoJ is still hiking and options already pay for yen calls, rather than EUR/USD, where the ECB's path is less certain. The strategic view should be built after the 2026-10-28 FOMC, when the tactical rally has played out, using 3-6 month options whose implied vol (6.10-6.31% in EUR/USD, 8.75% in USD/JPY at six months) is below the 1-month level.

consensus_divergence.our_view: We are Bullish the dollar for four weeks (EUR/USD 1.1100, DXY 103) and Bearish over six months (EUR/USD 1.1550, DXY 99.5 by March 2027). We agree with consensus on the direction of the six-month trend but not on its timing or size: the decline starts from a higher level and stops short of 1.18-1.20.
consensus_divergence.divergence_magnitude: Tactically about 700 pips against the 1.18 Q4 consensus path; strategically 250-450 pips less dollar weakness than MUFG (1.18-1.20) and Scotiabank (1.20-1.21) by Q1-Q2 2027.
consensus_divergence.why_we_differ: Consensus underweights the real-yield channel: a 10-year TIPS yield of 2.88% and a 2-year 90.5bp above the effective funds rate attract capital as long as US activity data stay strong, and the September data (GDP revised up to 2.2%, payrolls +162,000) argue that they will through October. It also underweights the energy shock's asymmetric effect: the US is a net energy exporter while the euro area and Japan are importers, so Brent near $103 helps US terms of trade. Over six months we agree that peer hikes and the twin deficits turn the dollar lower, but we think the ECB's path is less certain than consensus assumes, which caps EUR/USD near 1.16. The cleanest strategic short-dollar trade is therefore against the yen, not the euro.
consensus_divergence.payoff_if_right: A tactical long-dollar position in EUR/USD earns about 143 pips by late October; a strategic short-dollar position entered near 1.11 earns about 450 pips by March 2027, roughly 3% on the primary pair.
consensus_divergence.risk_if_wrong: If consensus is right on timing, the tactical position loses about 157 pips to the 1.1400 stop and the strategic view under-earns by 250-450 pips; if the dollar's rally becomes a left-side haven move, the strategic view loses about 293 pips to EUR/USD 1.0950.

cross_horizon_consistency.divergence_explanation: The divergence is mechanical. Over four weeks the heavily weighted Policy & Rates and Inflation & Growth factors are driven by data that have already printed and by real yields that are still rising, so the dollar's rate advantage dominates. Over six months the strategic weights shift toward External Balance (0.16), Guidance (0.12) and USD Liquidity (0.12), and Policy & Rates itself turns Neutral because the Fed is at its plateau while peers keep hiking, which lets the twin deficits and reserve diversification set the direction.

Policy-rate convention: the Fed is quoted as the 3.75-4.00% target range (upper bound 4.00% in the rate table) and all spreads and carry use the 3.875% midpoint; the euro uses the ECB deposit rate of 2.50% (MRO 2.65%); SGD carry uses the 6-month MAS T-bill (1.92%) as a proxy. Peer rates are the latest decision actuals: AUD 4.60, CAD 2.25, CHF 0.00, EUR 2.50, GBP 3.75, JPY 1.25, NOK 4.50, NZD 2.75, SEK 1.75.

Carry-to-vol uses 60-day realised vol recomputed through 2026-10-01 from the gated store (annualised on 252, weekday-only); where a CME 3-month implied vol exists it is shown alongside. No cross vol is built from USD legs.

Cross-currency basis is proxied by the CME futures calendar-spread roll premium minus the policy differential (2026-09-30); tenors are 19-47 days except CHF (75-166 days). No live XEURBI print was available.

CFTC: the cached TFF file has no DX contract; leveraged-fund and asset-manager USD positions are aggregated from EUR, JPY, GBP, CHF, CAD and AUD futures and converted at 2026-10-01 spot, which approximates historical notional. The IMM aggregate ($18.4bn) is from Saxo; the week to 2026-09-22 is the latest report published before the valuation date.
PPP table is a REER-relative proxy (USD BIS REER 106.70 divided by each peer's BIS REER, August 2026), not an absolute PPP model.

Macro table: GDP, unemployment and current account are point-in-time vintages as of 2026-10-01 except the US GDP q/q, which uses the 2026-09-30 third estimate (2.2% SAAR = 0.54% q/q), and US current account from BEA (-3.0%). CPI and core rows are the latest published prints (mostly August 2026) and were verified this run: US core PCE 3.0, EA 2.4, JP 1.7, UK 2.6, CH 0.4, CA 1.95 (BoC trim/median average), AU 3.6, NZ 2.7 (RBNZ sectoral factor; 30% trimmed mean 2.6% verified), NO 3.0, SE 0.5 (CPIF-XE), SG 2.2.

Balance-sheet runoff: the FOMC decided on 2025-10-29 to conclude runoff on 2025-12-01 (primary source); the cycle note's 2025-10-31 date is superseded by the Fed's statement.
